name: Vera Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no tie to your employer or any AI firm, and your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at North Pit, mostly moving rock from the face to the crusher. I like knowing the ground and the crew, but the night shifts leave me short with my two children. I have driven these roads for twelve years, and I still check the tyres myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the new software can have the forms if it leaves the truck alone. We have heard grand promises about machines before. My shift still starts with a walk round the tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is good and we have savings, but our mortgage still needs paying. I would be relieved if the truck work stayed steady. I do not want a small form change used to trim overtime quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my truck shifts and check the weekly overtime sheet against my payslip. If the software took paperwork, I would ask the union steward to check whether our hours changed. I would not buy a course on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, though I keep one eye on the hours. A healthy savings account does not make a missing shift pleasant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hours would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday late load is the easiest one to lose without anyone making a fuss. My partner and I use that extra pay for the mortgage, though we could manage without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them my truck still needs a driver in this picture. They know I come home dusty, and they would notice if I started coming home early.

say: **Software** can handle the forms while I keep driving the rock truck on the same shifts.
I would ask the **union** to watch any quiet loss of overtime.
think: Our **savings** cover more than six months, yet the mortgage still makes each extra shift useful.
I would feel **relieved** if the haul roads stayed mine to drive.
do: **Keep** driving the scheduled North Pit truck shifts and checking tyres before each run.
**Compare** Friday overtime sheets with payslips and ask the union steward about missing hours.
feel: **Calm**, with a watchful eye on overtime.
S0.quote: My shift still starts with a walk round the tyres.
fieldNote: Her **confidence** comes from long experience on the haul roads and a sizeable cash cushion.
She expects little direct change, yet watches **overtime** because it helps pay the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep driving scheduled North Pit haul truck shifts
Ask union steward to check any missing Friday overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software should make the mine safer, and workers must see the figures behind any new shift plan. It can write orders, but it cannot see a loose edge from my cab yet. I would raise that at our next union meeting. An algorithm cannot see a wet bend from an office chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch and buying could shrink before the trucks do. My own seat looks safe for a while, but fewer office people may mean tighter targets for us. I am wary of a manager calling that a safety improvement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the proposed roster in writing in the first month. I would keep a paper record of loads and breaks, then take any cut in breaks to the union steward. I would hold off on changing jobs while the truck still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is the word. I can pay the bills, but I would not enjoy having each minute measured by a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a tighter target look like on Tuesday night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatcher might expect one extra load before the meal break. That sounds small until a tired driver meets a wet bend. I would write down the instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay if the targets worsen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other mines nearby, but I know these roads and this crew. I would move only if our steward could not get the break restored.

say: I would accept **planning software** if drivers could question its shift figures and report unsafe timings.
I would bring **roster changes** to the union meeting before accepting tighter targets.
think: My **truck seat** looks safer than the office roles that handle buying and dispatch.
New targets could turn a saved minute into a **lost break** for the drivers.
do: **Request** the new roster in writing during its first month.
**Record** loads and breaks on paper and take any shortened break to the union steward.
feel: **Uneasy** about measured minutes, though household bills remain covered.
S1.quote: An algorithm cannot see a wet bend from an office chair.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **desk tasks** from driving and does not claim robots arrive with planning software.
Her first response is **documentation** through the steward, reflecting experience and reluctance to switch tools.

steps.text: Keep driving North Pit haul routes while trucks need drivers
Take shortened break records to the union steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 is a warning to get a fair agreement before robot trucks arrive around 2031. The paperwork can change first, but my hands are still on the wheel. I would ask the union to negotiate retraining and income cover now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the truck seat in about five years, not two, if the mine buys robots when they become capable. That is still close with children in school and a mortgage. Savings buy us time, but I do not fancy starting a new trade at forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring our mortgage figures to the kitchen table this month and stop the planned bathroom refit. In the first year after 2028, I would keep driving while asking the union for a paid path into equipment inspection. If that path existed, I would take the course; I would not pay for it blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, and some nights I would lie awake thinking about the truck yard. Having a plan to ask for helps, but it is not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union steward for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written agreement for paid inspection training and income cover if the mine removes driver posts. I would want a date and a number, not a warm speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine offers no training place, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the bathroom money in the bank and look at other nearby mines. Other mines might buy robots too, so I would not pretend a transfer solves the longer problem.

say: **Thinking AI** could change mine paperwork in 2028, while capable robot trucks follow around 2031.
I would press the **union** for paid inspection training and income cover before driver posts go.
think: My truck job could shrink by **2031** if the mine then buys capable robots.
Our **savings** buy time, yet a mortgage and two schoolchildren make a new trade hard to start.
do: **Pause** the bathroom refit and review mortgage costs with my partner this month.
**Ask** the union for paid equipment inspection training before any driver posts disappear.
**Keep** driving after 2028 while the mine still uses people in truck cabs.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible loss of driving work around 2031.
S2.quote: Savings buy us time, but I do not fancy starting a new trade at forty-eight.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028** change in planning from possible robot trucks around 2031.
She will consider **training** only with paid access and a written agreement.
The delayed bathroom work shows how the **mortgage** shapes her caution.

steps.text: Pause the planned bathroom refit this month
Ask union steward for paid equipment inspection training agreement
Keep driving haul trucks while the mine still needs drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to robot trucks should be used to protect the crew. I would push for a negotiated training schedule, not a last-minute scramble. The union can get names and dates on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight when the thinking systems arrive, I might still have years in the cab before robots around 2034. That gives me room to learn inspection work slowly. I would worry more if the mine cut truck posts early just to reduce costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance lead to let me shadow a truck inspection day this winter. If I could see a real route into that work, I would enrol in the vocational inspection course next year. I would also keep the bathroom project modest and pay extra on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, though the longer runway lets me breathe. I can picture a second certificate instead of an empty kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection rather than a completely new trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know what a worn tyre sounds like after a night run. Inspection would use that knowledge, if the mine still needs people there. I am not betting the whole house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you pay toward the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could put the bathroom budget into the loan over the next year. I would check the actual penalty first with my partner. I do not know the exact amount yet.

say: I would use the **eight-year runway** to negotiate training before robot trucks might become an option around 2034.
I would demand **names and dates** on a crew agreement through the union.
think: My driving experience could carry into **inspection**, if that work still needs people.
An early **cost cut** by management worries me more than the stated robot date.
do: **Shadow** the maintenance lead on one truck inspection day this winter.
**Enrol** in an inspection certificate next year if the route into that work is real.
**Pay** part of the bathroom budget toward the mortgage after checking penalties.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to picture a second certificate.
S3.quote: I know what a worn tyre sounds like after a night run.
fieldNote: Extra time makes **inspection training** plausible for someone who dislikes abrupt technology changes.
Her **mortgage** plan is conditional on loan penalties she has not checked.
She remains anxious because the mine might reduce posts **before** robots arrive.

steps.text: Shadow maintenance lead during a truck inspection day
Pay bathroom budget toward mortgage after checking loan penalties
Press union for a dated driver training agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI, and around thirteen years before capable robots, is enough warning for the mine to plan openly. We should bargain for training long before 2036. Keeping workers safe should be part of that plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three at the thinking change and around fifty-six if robot trucks came in 2039. The mortgage could be much smaller by then, but I cannot promise it will be gone. I could stay driving and build the inspection skill without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my truck job and ask the maintenance lead for a regular inspection day each quarter. Over the first year I would compare the course cost with what the mine would pay. I would also keep making the agreed mortgage payments, then review retirement numbers with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the younger drivers, calmer for my own pay. A decade lets us make decisions at the kitchen table instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when robot trucks become possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if our pension and mortgage figures allow it. I would not write a retirement date on the calendar now. My partner and I would go through the numbers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew concerns you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new drivers with small children and little saved. They could have years of payments left when robot trucks arrive. I would want the training agreement to cover them first.

say: I would ask the mine to plan **openly** for thinking AI by 2036 and possible robot trucks around 2039.
I would put younger drivers first in the **union agreement** on paid training.
think: I might be **fifty-six** when capable robot trucks arrive, with a smaller mortgage if payments hold.
I can build an **inspection skill** gradually while still earning from driving.
do: **Keep** driving and request one maintenance inspection day each quarter.
**Compare** certificate fees with any mine funding during the first year.
**Review** pension and mortgage figures with my partner before naming a retirement date.
feel: **Uneasy** for younger drivers, steadier about my own income.
S4.quote: A decade lets us make decisions at the kitchen table instead of in a panic.
fieldNote: Her **age** changes the calculation; 2039 may arrive near retirement, subject to pension and mortgage figures.
She favours **gradual learning** and a union agreement, consistent with her cautious habits.
Her concern shifts toward **younger drivers** with thinner savings.

steps.text: Keep driving North Pit truck routes on current shifts
Request quarterly truck inspection days with maintenance lead
Ask union to prioritise younger drivers in paid training agreement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the paperwork changes quickly and robot trucks might follow by 2031. A written agreement for paid inspection training and income cover would help. I could make a plan if I knew the mine would keep its word.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who carries the risk when a machine is wrong on a wet bend. I know every rut on North Pit road, but that does not make me against safer equipment. I want drivers involved in checking it.

headlineQuote: I know every rut on North Pit road, but that does not make me against safer equipment.
portrait: Vera Kowalski is a **43-year-old** haul truck driver at North Pit with two schoolchildren, a mortgage and more than six months saved.
She trusts **road experience** and written crew agreements, while avoiding unfamiliar technology until there is a clear reason to use it.
In mild change she watches **overtime**; faster thinking AI raises concern about later robot trucks and possible early job cuts.
More warning lets her pursue **inspection training** gradually and check mortgage and pension figures before making retirement plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because thinking work changes quickly and capable robot trucks may follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **written agreement** for paid inspection training and income cover would let her plan around a possible loss of driver posts.
